subject: chemistry
question_text: Give an account of VSEPR theory and its applications.

verification.note: Chapter 3 is sourced from the Sri Chaitanya Junior Fastrack chemistry section (book pp.56-61), which prints the question, its star rank and a model answer. Only ONE source book is held for chemistry — the TSBIE Basic Learning Material in hand covers physics only — so the two-book union check is PENDING a second chemistry source. The 4+2+1+1 mark split is a CLAIM until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it; the question itself is sourced, not invented. The book's six postulates are grouped into two marked steps of two marks each; the book's H₂O angle 104°30′ equals the 104.5° that NCERT prints — both notations are correct and the card uses 104°30′ with 104.5° in brackets once.

steps.label: Postulates — shape from repulsions
lines: VSEPR theory (valence shell electron pair
repulsion theory) — postulates:
1. The shape of a molecule is decided by
the repulsions between ALL the electron
pairs — bond pairs and lone pairs — in the
valence shell of the central atom.
2. The electron pairs arrange themselves
around the central atom so that the
repulsions among them are minimum.
steps.why: These two postulates are the core of the theory: count every electron pair on the central atom, then place the pairs as far apart as the geometry allows.
common_mistakes: Counting only bond pairs. Lone pairs count too, and they are the reason NH₃ and H₂O are not tetrahedral.
Writing maximum repulsion. The pairs settle where repulsion is MINIMUM.
steps.memory_tip: Count all pairs, spread all pairs — the two sentences of the theory.
steps.margin_note: Expand the name VSEPR in full once at the start.

steps.label: Postulates — lone pair rules
lines: 3. A lone pair occupies more space than a
bond pair, because it belongs to one atom
only.
4. The order of repulsions is:
LP–LP > LP–BP > BP–BP.
5. The magnitude of repulsion between bond
pairs depends on the electronegativity
difference between the central atom and
the bonded atoms.
6. Repulsion strength of multiple bonds:
triple > double > single.
steps.why: The lone pair postulates are what give the theory its predictions: extra repulsion from lone pairs compresses the angles between bond pairs, which the two applications below use.
common_mistakes: Reversing the repulsion order. Lone pair against lone pair is the STRONGEST repulsion.
Writing BP–BP as the strongest because bonds seem solid. Bond pairs repel least.
steps.memory_tip: The freer the pair, the more room it takes: LP–LP strongest, BP–BP weakest.
steps.margin_note: The inequality LP–LP > LP–BP > BP–BP is the most-quoted line of this answer.

steps.label: Application — NH₃
lines: Application 1 — NH₃:
N undergoes sp³ hybridisation and has
three bond pairs and ONE lone pair.
The lone pair repels the bond pairs more
strongly than they repel each other.
The bond angle is reduced from 109°28′
The shape changes from tetrahedral to
pyramidal.
steps.why: NH₃ shows the theory working once: one lone pair pushes the three N−H bonds closer together, so both the angle and the shape name change from the pure tetrahedral case.
common_mistakes: Calling NH₃ trigonal planar. The lone pair sits on the fourth sp³ position, so the shape is pyramidal.
Writing 107° without the starting value 109°28′. The reduction IS the application.
steps.memory_tip: One lone pair: angle down about two degrees, shape pyramidal.
steps.margin_note: State both angles — the starting 109°28′ and the reduced 107°.

steps.label: Application — H₂O
lines: Application 2 — H₂O:
O undergoes sp³ hybridisation and has
two bond pairs and TWO lone pairs.
The two lone pairs repel more strongly, so
the bond angle is reduced further, from
The shape changes from tetrahedral to
bent (angular).
steps.why: H₂O shows the same effect doubled: two lone pairs compress the angle more than one did in NH₃, and only two bonded atoms remain visible, so the shape reads as bent.
common_mistakes: Calling H₂O linear. The two lone pairs bend it to 104°30′.
Writing one lone pair for oxygen. Oxygen keeps TWO lone pairs in water.
steps.memory_tip: Two lone pairs: angle down twice as far, shape bent.
steps.margin_note: 104°30′ and 104.5° are the same angle written two ways.

steps.label: The diagrams
steps.why: The two sketches make the argument visible: the dots above N and O are the lone pairs doing the compressing, and the marked angles show the result on each molecule.
common_mistakes: Leaving the lone pair dots off. Without them the drawn shapes have no cause.
Marking 109°28′ on these molecules. That angle belongs to CH₄; here the angles are 107° and 104°30′.
steps.memory_tip: Dots on top, squeezed angle below — one pair of dots for NH₃, two for H₂O.
steps.margin_note: Draw the lone pairs as dots ABOVE the central atom; label each angle.

steps.label: Summary
lines: Zero, one, two lone pairs — each added
lone pair reduces the bond angle further.
steps.why: The three-angle ladder compresses the whole answer into one comparable line, which is also the form short questions on VSEPR take.
common_mistakes: Attaching the angles to the wrong molecules when writing quickly. Pair them: CH₄ largest, H₂O smallest.
steps.memory_tip: 109, 107, 104 — the angle steps down as the lone pairs count up.
steps.margin_note: Unmarked closing line; it makes the two applications read as one pattern.

insider_note: The angle ladder 109°28′, 107°, 104°30′ carries the application marks — one added lone pair reduces the angle each time, and all three numbers must appear.
